title: Week 26 Check-In · By the Great Horn Spoon!
description: This week you read Chapters 4 to 6 and studied how Fleischman makes you laugh. You practiced dialogue punctuation and paragraphing, the roots rid/ris and lud/lus, dialogue tags and spelling in quoted speech, and drafting a scene with voice. Show what you know.

questions.label: Identification
options: “It’s that boy”, he shouted, waving the meat cleaver.
“It’s that boy,” he shouted, waving the meat cleaver.
“It’s that boy,” He shouted, waving the meat cleaver.
“It’s that boy” he shouted waving the meat cleaver.
questions.status: fixed (four options; the book's exact line)

questions.label: Correction
questions.text: Fix the punctuation and paragraphing. Each speaker needs a new paragraph.
questions.excerpt: Stuff and nonsense Praiseworthy would say even though he believed every word of it. Well said Mr. Azariah Jones I hope he doesn't try that.
questions.key: “Stuff and nonsense,” Praiseworthy would say, even though he believed every word of it. / (new paragraph) “Well,” said Mr. Azariah Jones, “I hope he doesn’t try that.”

questions.label: Application
questions.text: Write a 3-line dialogue set aboard the Lady Wilma. Use quotation marks, commas inside the closing marks, and a new paragraph for each new speaker.
questions.key: Three lines, correct marks, new paragraph per speaker.
questions.from: 26.2 Grammar Show What You Know; 26.3 Grammar

questions.label: Root
questions.text: Which word contains a root meaning play or jest?

questions.label: Context Clues
questions.text: Read the sentence from Chapter 6. What does monotony mean?
questions.excerpt: “Even a haircut broke the monotony of these endless days at sea.”
options: Boring sameness, with nothing new happening
questions.status: new (vocabulary in context; replaces a second root-meaning item)

questions.label: Use the Word
questions.text: Use the word ludicrous in a sentence about this week's chapters. Then tell how its root lud (play) helps explain its meaning.
questions.key: A sentence using ludicrous correctly + lud = play/jest, so something laughable like a joke.

questions.label: Identification
questions.text: Which dialogue tag is spelled correctly?

questions.label: Spelling in Quoted Speech
questions.text: In Chapter 4, Mountain Jim says a bit of singing will pass the time. Which spelling shows how he says it?
questions.status: new (the scope's quoted-speech half; replaces bellowed in syllables)

questions.label: Tag Choice
questions.text: A character speaks quietly and grumpily, under their breath. Which dialogue tag fits best?
questions.status: kept (a fourth option added; the written explanation dropped)

questions.label: Comprehension
questions.text: How does Jack's time as a stowaway lead to the solution in Chapter 6?
options: He hid in the potato barrels and sucked the potatoes, so he knew they were juicy enough to keep grape cuttings alive.
He ran away from home, so he understood how Monsieur Gaunt felt.
He was small, so he could reach the potatoes deep in the hold.
He was ship's boy, so he knew where the fresh water was kept.

questions.label: Inference
questions.text: Read the line from Chapter 5. Why does Praiseworthy say “Stuff and nonsense” if he believes the stories? What does this show about his role among the passengers?
questions.key: He keeps calm on the outside to steady the frightened passengers; he is a calm leader (self-control).

questions.label: Humor Analysis
questions.text: Choose one comic moment from Chapters 4–6. Name the technique that makes it funny (comic contrast, the straight face, or the ticking clock) and explain in 2–3 sentences.
questions.key: A real moment + a named technique + how it works.

questions.label: Read Like a Writer
questions.text: In this line, a reaction sits in the middle of the speech, set off by commas. Write one line for your own scene the same way: dialogue, a reaction, then more dialogue.
questions.excerpt: “You mean to say, sir,” said Mr. Azariah Jones, turning white, “that we’ve been bouncing around in that awful place?” (Chapter 5)
questions.key: Speech + tag with a reaction set off by commas + more speech, punctuated correctly.
questions.status: new (the scope's Read Like a Writer focus)

questions.label: Your Scene
questions.text: Copy 4–6 sentences from your adventure scene. Include correctly punctuated dialogue, one of this week's dialogue tags, and a moment that shows your hero's voice.
questions.key: Dialogue punctuated correctly + a tag from the list + a voice moment.
